content:
Have you ever turned on the radio and felt that every pop song sounds alike? Or watched a horror film and figured out the ending within 20 minutes?

In a new paper published in *Frontiers in Psychology*, researchers from Singapore Management University and James Cook University Singapore point out that 'hyperselection' refers to how, under intense competition, humans become increasingly adept at identifying and optimising what works, continually choosing the same traits rather than trying other options.

The result is a blow to creativity. In a world that increasingly demands optimisation, hyperselection could make everything from music to urban design to football matches more monotonous.

Jose C. Yong, a research psychologist and the paper's lead author, likens hyperselection to natural selection—the evolutionary process whereby individuals with advantageous traits or more effective strategies are more likely to survive and reproduce. Modern technology has made this selection process extremely fast and intense.

"Now we can instantly identify which is performing best, almost immediately copy it, and then keep optimising," Yong said. "When there is strong selection pressure, such as intense competition or serious consequences for not optimising, this process accelerates."

Optimisation is generally useful because it helps us achieve goals more efficiently. But when everyone is optimising for the same thing, other traits, behaviours, products, and strategies may disappear, 'replacing diversity or variation—which could be more adaptive and useful—with efficiency.'

When we engage in hyperselection, we lose creative masterworks like "Bohemian Rhapsody."

When explaining the concept of hyperselection to those unfamiliar with it, Yong likes to cite Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody." Contemporary reviews from 1975 initially criticised the song as an "audacious pastiche" and a "discordant collage of styles," but the single is now considered one of the greatest works in rock history, largely because the band dared to take creative risks.

"Bohemian Rhapsody is the opposite of hyperselection."

"The song runs nearly six minutes long, spans wildly different musical sections, has no conventional chorus, and includes an operatic segment—it really stands out," Yong said.

Another clearly non-hyperselected song is Stevie Nicks's "Edge of Seventeen," which breaks with traditional song structure and has an extremely recognisable sound. Yong also mentions System of a Down, saying their songs sound "completely out of this world" yet still became chart-toppers "because they were fresh and unique enough."

Compared with the past, today's radio pop songs could be described as derivative and boring, and Yong even struggles to name one particularly distinctive track to use as an example.

"To be honest, I'm not sure I can cite a current pop song as an example of hyperselection, partly because so many of today's pop songs sound similar and none of them leave a deep impression," he said.

But he says certain music genres are perfect embodiments of hyperselection. For example, the gloomy, melancholic pop sung by artists whispering softly, or the mumble-rap that was ubiquitous a few years back.

Hyperselection also explains why Yong's co-author and fellow research psychologist Edison Tan barely listens to the radio, instead seeking out newer, less-played independent musicians.

"It's not that my tastes have changed—it's the world that has changed," Tan told HuffPost. "I crave rich and nuanced emotional expression, and pop music can no longer provide it."

Yong said that, driven by metrics such as streaming view counts, marketing reach, and the fleeting attention spans of social media, music has become shorter and simpler, a trend already extensively documented in the literature.

Beyond music, where else is hyperselection appearing?

Yong, Tan, and their co-author Simon S. Groome say that hyperselection—the pursuit of optimisation and efficiency—has made nearly every sphere of life more predictable, formulaic, and dull. They see this phenomenon in sports as well.

In professional football, teams are constantly seeking tactics that can give them an edge. Once a strategy proves effective, opponents quickly follow suit. Matches have become more competitive and tactically sophisticated, but teams' playing styles are also increasingly similar, leaving less room for individual flair.

Careers are no exception. Tan uses academia, a field he is familiar with, as an example.

"When we were in graduate school, we were taught to think boldly, explore new ideas, and understand how the world works," he said.

In an ideal world, the best researchers would be the most creative problem-solvers—people willing to be different. But reality falls far short of this ideal.

"Scholars are forced to prove their worth through metrics like publication counts, citation numbers, and how much funding they secure through research grants, rather than the inherent value of their ideas," Tan said.

He added: "The 'P' in PhD, which stands for philosophy, has long lost its meaning. When we see the same pattern emerging in every aspect of life, we wonder whether there is some fundamental force driving these trends."

AI will accelerate hyperselection

It almost goes without saying that AI will accelerate hyperselection, Yong said. AI is itself designed for recursive optimisation with minimal human intervention, and it operates at speeds and scales far beyond human or previous technological capabilities.

"We're already seeing this with online content—AI-generated articles, ad copy, social media posts, images, videos, website designs, even music all feel extremely similar because they are generated from the same underlying patterns and continually optimised based on what works," he said.

If people consume this content uncritically, there will be virtually no counterbalancing force against AI-driven hyperselection.

Hyperselection isn't entirely bad, but creators should be mindful of this phenomenon.

Yong stresses that optimisation itself is not bad—it can help people achieve goals and improve their lives. But because the pressure to optimise can be intense, creators may unwittingly sacrifice adaptive variety.

"That's why it's important to be aware of hyperselection, and that's why I want to articulate this concept clearly—because if we can recognise it, we can think about what to do when it occurs," he said.

The key, Yong says, is understanding how easily we fall into the trap of hyperselection and finding ways to nurture creativity and preserve diversity.

"Creativity often comes from exposure to different things, then combining them in new ways. If everything looks, sounds, and feels the same, we lose the reservoir of alternative strategies and the raw material from which new ideas can be born," he said.

We also need to think more critically about what we consume.

"If audiences can recognise when music, films, or other cultural products have become too formulaic and demand something more interesting, that in itself will change the selection pressures influencing production," Yong said.
